extracted.intended_audience: Employers, human-resources professionals, employment lawyers, small business owners, and stakeholders affected by or commenting on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory text establishing definitions, prohibitions, notice requirements, exceptions, and PRA/compliance-cost estimates for the FTC's final rule banning most non-compete clauses and requiring notice for existing non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compete clause (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term or condition of employment that prohibits a worker from, penalizes a worker for, or functions to prevent a worker from: (i) seeking or accepting work in the United States with a different person where such work would begin after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition; or (ii) operating a business in the United States after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of this part, 'term or condition of employment' includes, but is not limited to, a contractual term or workplace policy, whether written or oral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Worker means a natural person who works or who previously worked, whether paid or unpaid, without regard to the worker's title or the worker's status under any other State or Federal laws, including, but not limited to, whether the worker is an employee, independent contractor, extern, intern, volunteer, apprentice, or a sole proprietor who provides a service to a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term includes a natural person who works for a franchisee or franchisor, but does not include a franchisee in the context of a franchisee-franchisor relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior executive (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior executive means a worker who: (1) was in a policy-making position; and (2) received from a person for the employment total annual compensation of at least $151,164 in the preceding year (with specific rules for annualizing compensation for partial-year employment or departures prior to the preceding year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition ties senior executive status to both policy-making position and a compensation threshold; the rule uses this to limit notice/enforcement obligations for certain executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total annual compensation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total annual compensation is based on the worker's earnings over the preceding year and may include salary, commissions, nondiscretionary bonuses and other nondiscretionary compensation earned during that 52-week period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total annual compensation does not include board, lodging and other facilities as defined in 29 CFR 541.606, and does not include payments for medical insurance, payments for life insurance, contributions to retirement plans and the cost of other similar fringe benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-making authority / position (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy-making authority means final authority to make policy decisions that control significant aspects of a business entity. Policy-making position means a business entity's president, chief executive officer or equivalent, any other officer who has policy-making authority, or any other natural person who has policy-making authority similar to an officer with policy-making authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-making authority does not include authority limited to advising or exerting influence; officers of subsidiaries or affiliates may be deemed policy-making for purposes of the common enterprise; a person without policy-making authority over a common enterprise may not be deemed to have a policy-making position even if they have such authority over a subsidiary or affiliate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited conduct re: workers other than senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a worker other than a senior executive, it is an unfair method of competition for a person: (i) to enter into or attempt to enter into a non-compete clause; (ii) to enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause; or (iii) to represent that the worker is subject to a non-compete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a broad prohibition covering creation, enforcement, and representations regarding non-competes for non-senior-executive workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited conduct re: senior executives (post-effective-date)
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a senior executive, it is an unfair method of competition for a person: (i) to enter into or attempt to enter into a non-compete clause; (ii) to enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause entered into after the effective date; or (iii) to represent that the senior executive is subject to a non-compete clause, where the non-compete clause was entered into after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule treats existing non-competes for senior executives differently (existing senior-executive non-competes are not subject to the same notice/ unenforceability treatment as those entered after the effective date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice required for existing non-compete clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: For each existing non-compete clause that it is unfair to enforce under the rule (i.e., existing non-competes for workers other than senior executives), the person who entered into the non-compete must provide clear and conspicuous notice to the worker by the effective date that the worker's non-compete clause will not be, and cannot legally be, enforced against the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice obligation is a one-time requirement by the effective date; the rule intends this to be simple and to minimize legal assistance needs for employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of notice (required contents and delivery methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice must (i) identify the person who entered into the non-compete clause with the worker and (ii) be on paper delivered by hand, or by mail to the worker's last known personal street address, or by email at an email address belonging to the worker (including current work or last known personal email), or by text message to a mobile telephone number belonging to the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section §910.2(b)(2) sets these as acceptable delivery methods; employers may choose among them. The rule also permits providing notice electronically and anticipates many employers will do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception when no contact information exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person required to provide notice has no record of a street address, email address, or mobile telephone number for a worker, that person is exempt from the notice requirement with respect to that worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to reduce burdens where employers cannot reasonably contact a worker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model language constitutes notice (safe harbor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The model language provided in §910.2(b)(4) constitutes notice to the worker that the worker's non-compete clause cannot legally be enforced and will not be enforced against the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing the model language is a safe harbor: §910.2(b)(5) states that a person complies with the notice requirement if they provide notice pursuant to the model language. Employers may use the model language to minimize compliance uncertainty and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional notice in additional languages / translations
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to providing the required notice in English, a person is permitted (but not required) to provide the notice in one or more other languages or include internet links to translations in additional languages. A person may use any Commission-provided translation of the model language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing translations is optional and not required; employers that choose to provide translations may use Commission-provided translations of the model language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona fide sale of business exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of this part do not apply to a non-compete clause that is entered into by a person pursuant to a bona fide sale of a business entity, of the person's ownership interest in a business entity, or of all or substantially all of a business entity's operating assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit statutory example of an exception preserving standard business sale practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing causes of action exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of this part do not apply where a cause of action related to a non-compete clause accrued prior to the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-existing litigation rights/causes of action are preserved and not displaced by the new rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith enforcement exception
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an unfair method of competition to enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause or to make representations about a non-compete clause where a person has a good-faith basis to believe that this part is inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a limited defense where an employer reasonably believes the rule does not apply to the conduct at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to State laws and preservation of State authority and private rights
rubrics_metrics.description: This part will not be construed to annul or exempt any person from complying with any State statute, regulation, order, or interpretation applicable to a non-compete clause, except that this part supersedes such laws to the extent those laws would otherwise permit or authorize conduct that is an unfair method under §910.2(a) or conflict with the notice requirement in §910.2(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for laws superseded to the limited extent described, the rule preserves State attorney general authority and private rights of action; it does not alter, limit, or affect state enforcement authorities or private claims arising under state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is effective 120 days after publication in the Federal Register (stated as September 4, 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must comply by the effective date (e.g., providing notice by that date for existing non-competes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) requirements for information collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PRA, Federal agencies must obtain OMB approval for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor; collections must display a valid control number assigned by OMB; agencies may not conduct or sponsor, and persons are not required to respond to, an information collection unless it displays a valid control number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission evaluated whether the notice requirement constituted a PRA collection and finalized the notice requirement largely as proposed with adjustments to ease compliance; the PRA framework constrains how the Commission treats the notice as a collection of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance time and cost assumptions used in RIA/FRFA
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumed times and unit costs used for estimating compliance burdens: composing/sending a digital notice takes 20 minutes of an HR specialist's time (median HR wage $31.85/hour → $21.23 per establishment); mailed notice cost per notice estimated at $1.81 (5¢ printing + 70¢ postage + 1 minute HR at $63.70/hour). Updating contractual practices assumed to require 4–8 hours of attorney time at $134.62/hour, yielding $538.48–$1,076.96 per firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission describes these assumptions as averages and notes substantial heterogeneity across firms; it also uses a conservative assumption that each establishment must engage in its own communication (i.e., headquarters cannot send a single company-wide notice) for upper-bound estimates. Aggregate estimates derived: total mailed notice and digital-notice burdens and total-update costs range given (e.g., $1.4B–$2.8B for contract-updating at national level under the 4–8 hour assumption).
